blocks.text: 12.2.1 Schemas for Model Inputs

Every planning cycle, GridCap's planning database exports one JSON document for the optimization service: the years, the budgets, the crews, the regional floors and the 40 candidate projects. The service builds the model from it, solves, and stores the result with the scenario (lesson 12.1.4). Last cycle the export team renamed one column. Nothing crashed, and one child project quietly lost its one-year lag behind its parent. This lesson puts a schema at the door of the service, so that a document like that is refused, with the reason, before any model is built. GridCap is a fictional utility; its numbers describe no real company.

Lesson 1.3.2 introduced pydantic on one CSV row at a time: `BaseModel`, field types and bounds, field and model validators, and `ValidationError`. This lesson uses the same tools on a different unit: the whole snapshot, as it crosses the boundary between two programs. A **snapshot** is one complete set of model inputs, frozen at one moment; lesson 7.1.3 gave each scenario a snapshot id, and lesson 12.2.3 shows how that id is computed. A **schema** is the written rule for what a valid snapshot looks like: which keys, which types, which bounds, and which references must resolve.

The course's runner has pydantic 2.14.1 and no other schema library (pandera, for one, is not installed), and FastAPI, which lesson 12.4.1 uses for the service, builds on pydantic. So the schema is a set of pydantic models.
The Schema Is the Model's Sets and Parameters, Written as Types

A schema for model inputs is not designed from the file. It is read off the model: every set and every parameter the model uses becomes a field, and every assumption the model makes about them becomes a type, a bound or a rule. Here is the planning model the service solves (section 6's multi-period model; lesson 12.2.2 restates it, and its program is `plan_model.py`).

**Sets.** $`Y`$ the plan's years, in order; $`P`$ the candidate projects; $`T_i`$ the start years of project $`i`$: the years $`t`$ with $`e_i \le t \le l_i`$ whose work ends inside the plan, $`t + d_i - 1 \le \max Y`$; $`M \subseteq P`$ the must-do projects; $`\mathcal{G}`$ the alternative groups, each a set of projects; $`C \subseteq P`$ the child projects, each with parent $`p(c)`$ and lag $`L_c`$ years; $`Q`$ the programs (transmission, distribution, vegetation), with $`q(i)`$ the program of project $`i`$; $`R`$ the regions, with $`r(i)`$ the region of project $`i`$.

**Parameters.** $`e_i, l_i`$, project $`i`$'s earliest and latest start year; $`c_{i,k}`$, what project $`i`$ spends in its $`k`$-th year of work, $`k = 0, \dots, d_i - 1`$, where $`d_i`$ is its number of years of work ($k); $`\text{capex}_i = \sum_k c_{i,k}`$ ($k); $`\text{npv}_{i,t}`$, its NPV if it starts in year $`t`$ ($k); $`m_i`$, the crew-months it needs in each year of work; $`B_y`$, the budget of year $`y`$ ($k); $`K_{q,y}`$, the crew-months program $`q`$ has in year $`y`$; $`\text{floor}_r`$, the least region $`r`$ must receive over the plan ($k).
**Variables.** $`x_{i,t} \in \{0, 1\}`$ for every $`i \in P`$ and $`t \in T_i`$: project $`i`$ starts in year $`t`$.
**Objective.**
\max \; \sum_{i \in P} \sum_{t \in T_i} \text{npv}_{i,t}\, x_{i,t}
**Constraints.**

\begin{aligned}
\sum_{t \in T_i} x_{i,t} &\le 1 && \forall i \in P \setminus M && \text{(once}_i) \\
\sum_{t \in T_i} x_{i,t} &= 1 && \forall i \in M && \text{(must}_i) \\
\sum_{i \in g} \sum_{t \in T_i} x_{i,t} &\le 1 && \forall g \in \mathcal{G} && \text{(alt}_g) \\
\sum_{u \in T_c,\, u \le t} x_{c,u} &\le \sum_{s \in T_{p(c)},\, s \le t - L_c} x_{p(c),s} && \forall c \in C,\ t \in T_c && \text{(after}_{c,t}) \\
\sum_{i \in P} \sum_{t \in T_i,\, 0 \le y - t < d_i} c_{i,\,y-t}\, x_{i,t} &\le B_y && \forall y \in Y && \text{(budget}_y) \\
\sum_{i:\, q(i) = q} \ \sum_{t \in T_i,\, 0 \le y - t < d_i} m_i\, x_{i,t} &\le K_{q,y} && \forall q \in Q,\ y \in Y && \text{(crews}_{q,y}) \\
\sum_{i:\, r(i) = r} \ \sum_{t \in T_i} \text{capex}_i\, x_{i,t} &\ge \text{floor}_r && \forall r \in R && \text{(floor}_r)
\end{aligned}
Each line of the model asks something of the data, and the schema writes it down:

rows: $`c_{i,k} \ge 0`$ in whole $k, at least one year of work
$`e_i \le l_i`$, so the window holds a year
$`i \in M`$ only on a real yes
$`p(c) \in P`$, one variable family per project
$`K_{q,y}`$ for every $`q \in Q`$, $`y \in Y`$, exactly once

blocks.text: The discount rate is in the snapshot too ($`0 < \text{rate} < 1`$), although this model reads the NPVs directly: the reports of section 7 use it, and a snapshot holds every input of the run.
The project record is the row model of lesson 1.3.2 grown to everything the model reads, and the snapshot nests it with the year, crew and floor records:

class ProjectIn(Contract):
    project_id: str = Field(pattern=r"^P\d{3}$")
    program: Program
    region: Region
    cost_profile: tuple[NonNegativeInt, ...] = Field(min_length=1)    # $k per year of work
    earliest_start: int
    latest_start: int
    must_do: bool
    parent: str | None = None
    parent_lag: NonNegativeInt = 0                                     # years after the parent starts
    alt_group: str | None = None
    crew_months: NonNegativeInt                                        # per year of work
    npv: tuple[int, ...]                                               # $k, one per start year in the window

class Snapshot(Contract):
    schema_version: Literal[1]
    name: str
    years: tuple[int, ...] = Field(min_length=1)
    discount_rate: float = Field(gt=0, lt=1)
    budget: tuple[YearAmount, ...]
    crews: tuple[CrewLimit, ...]
    region_floor: tuple[RegionFloor, ...]
    projects: tuple[ProjectIn, ...]

A field whose type is another model, such as `budget: tuple[YearAmount, ...]`, is a **nested model**: pydantic validates each record of the list as a `YearAmount`. `YearAmount` has two fields, `year: int` and `amount: NonNegativeInt`; `CrewLimit` and `RegionFloor` are built the same way. Budgets, crews and floors are lists of records rather than dicts keyed by year, because JSON keys are always strings: a record keeps the year an integer and gives each value a name. `Contract` is the base class every part shares; the third section shows what it sets.
The export of GridCap small, sent as JSON text and validated in one call, `load(text)`, which is `Snapshot.model_validate_json(text)`:

11,362 bytes -> Snapshot: 40 projects, 5 years, 5 budgets, 15 crew limits, 4 floors
P039: (1170, 880) True (546, 386, 252)

What comes back is one frozen object whose every part has the type the model needs: P039's cost profile is a tuple of integers, its must-do flag a boolean, and its NPVs one per start year from 2027 to 2029.
One Schema Validates the Whole Snapshot and Reports Every Problem in One Pass
`schema_whole.py` plants errors in a copy of the export. First, five at once:

bad = copy.deepcopy(doc)
project(bad, "P007")["cost_profile"] = [2140, -720]          # a credit typed as a cost
project(bad, "P012")["region"] = "Coastal"                   # a region the model has no floor for
project(bad, "P030")["npv"] = [4374]                         # one NPV for a two-year window
bad["budget"][1]["amount"] = None                             # a blank cell
project(bad, "P016")["parent"] = "P099"                       # a parent that is not in the snapshot

4 problems in one pass:
   budget.1.amount | Input should be a valid integer
   projects.6.cost_profile.1 | Input should be greater than or equal to 0
   projects.11.region | Input should be 'Ridge', 'Valley', 'Coast' or 'Plains'
   projects.29 | Value error, npv needs one value per start year of the window
P016's unknown parent reported: False

Pydantic does not stop at the first bad field: it validates every field of every record and returns all the failures in one `ValidationError`, each with its location. `budget.1.amount` is the amount of the second budget record; `projects.6.cost_profile.1` is the second year of work of the seventh project, P007. A sender fixes all four in one round instead of four.

Four, not five. The unknown parent P099 is a rule across records, written as a model validator on `Snapshot` (below), and an after-validator runs only on a model whose fields all passed. So the problems come in two layers: field problems first, and reference problems once the fields are clean. P030's problem is reported because it is a model validator of `ProjectIn`, whose own fields were all valid.
The references are the rules no single record can break. Each says that something the model will look up exists, exactly once:

@model_validator(mode="after")
    def references_resolve(self):
        """Every id and key the model will look up exists, exactly once. All problems at once."""
        problems = []
        ids = Counter(p.project_id for p in self.projects)
        problems += [f"project {pid} appears {n} times" for pid, n in sorted(ids.items()) if n > 1]
        problems += [f"{p.project_id}: parent {p.parent} is not a project"
                     for p in self.projects if p.parent and p.parent not in ids]
        years = Counter(b.year for b in self.budget)
        problems += [f"year {y}: {years[y]} budget rows" for y in self.years if years[y] != 1]
        crews = Counter((c.program, c.year) for c in self.crews)
        problems += [f"{q} {y}: {crews[q, y]} crew rows" for q in Program.__args__ for y in self.years
                     if crews[q, y] != 1]
        if problems:
            raise ValueError("; ".join(problems))
        return self

`Counter` (from `collections`) counts how often each key occurs, and gives 0 for a key it never saw, so "missing" and "twice" are the same test: a count other than 1. `Program.__args__` is the tuple of names in the `Literal` type. The validator collects every problem before it raises, for the same reason pydantic collects field errors. Four reference errors, planted together:

1 error at loc ():
   project P001 appears 2 times
   P016: parent P099 is not a project
   year 2031: 0 budget rows
   vegetation 2030: 0 crew rows
The location `()` is the empty tuple: the error belongs to the whole snapshot, not to a field.

Each of these would otherwise fail later, and worse. `plan_model.py` keeps the projects in a dict by id, so of a project exported twice, whichever copy comes last silently wins, even when the two copies disagree on its cost. It reads the budget as `budget[y]`, so a missing 2031 raises a `KeyError` deep inside the model build, with no word about the export. A builder written with `budget.get(y, 0)` would be worse still: it would set $`B_{2031} = 0`$ and solve a model in which nothing can be spent in 2031.

The schema's job ends here: if a snapshot passes, the model can be built from it, every set and parameter present and well typed. Whether the model then has a plan, and whether the numbers are believable, is the job of lesson 12.2.2.
<!-- practice 1 -->
At a Machine Boundary, Forbid Unknown Keys and Turn Off Guessing

Lesson 1.3.2 used pydantic's defaults, which suit a person's spreadsheet: unknown columns are ignored, and a string that clearly means a number is converted (**lax** mode). The service's sender is a program, and every surprise in its output is a bug in that program. Two settings make the schema say so. Both sit on the base class that every part of the snapshot inherits:

`extra="forbid"` refuses a key the model does not declare (the default, `"ignore"`, drops it). `strict=True` turns off conversion: a value must already have its field's JSON type. Both can be overridden for one call (`model_validate_json(text, extra="ignore")`, `strict=False`), which `schema_boundary.py` uses to put the two policies side by side. First, last cycle's export, in which P023's `parent_lag` column arrived renamed to `lag`:

P023 sends 'lag' instead of 'parent_lag'
  extra='ignore'  accepted, P023 parent_lag=0, P001 must_do=False, 2027 budget=8890
  extra='forbid'  refused: projects.22.lag: Extra inputs are not permitted

With `"ignore"` the document is accepted. `lag` is dropped as unknown, `parent_lag` is missing, and its default fills the gap: P023's lag becomes 0. In the model, that changes the rows $`\text{after}_{\text{P023},t}`$: P023 may now start in the same year as its parent P022, not a year later. No error, no warning, a different plan. A default on a field is convenient for a person typing a document and dangerous for a program sending one, because a renamed key turns into the default without a sound. With `"forbid"`, the same document is refused and the message names the key.
Next, four ways an exporter can send a number or a flag in the wrong JSON type:

budget 8890 sent as "8890"
  strict=False    accepted, P023 parent_lag=1, P001 must_do=False, 2027 budget=8890
  strict=True     refused: budget.0.amount: Input should be a valid integer
budget 8890 sent as 8890.0
  strict=False    accepted, P023 parent_lag=1, P001 must_do=False, 2027 budget=8890
  strict=True     refused: budget.0.amount: Input should be a valid integer
budget 8890 sent as 8890.5
  strict=False    refused: budget.0.amount: Input should be a valid integer, got a number with a fractional part
  strict=True     refused: budget.0.amount: Input should be a valid integer
P001 must_do sent as "no"
  strict=False    accepted, P023 parent_lag=1, P001 must_do=False, 2027 budget=8890
  strict=True     refused: projects.0.must_do: Input should be a valid boolean

Lax mode converts every one it can read without losing information, and here each conversion happens to give the right value. That is the problem: an exporter that writes budgets as strings, or flags as `"no"`, has a bug that will one day write something lax mode reads differently from what was meant. Lesson 1.3.2's lax rules are right for a planner's CSV, where every cell is text. Between two programs that both speak JSON, a string where a number belongs is never right, and strict mode says so the first time it happens.

Strict mode checks values against **JSON** types when it validates JSON text. A JSON array is the JSON form of a tuple, so `years: [2027, ...]` passes. The export's Python dict, validated as Python data with `model_validate`, is refused, because there a Python `list` is not a `tuple`:
the export's Python dict, strict: years | Input should be a valid tuple
So the service validates what it receives, the JSON text, with `model_validate_json`, and never a dict that some other code built from it.
The Schema Is a Versioned Contract, Published as JSON Schema

A schema the sender cannot read is a rule they find out about by being refused. Pydantic writes each model out as a **JSON Schema**, a standard JSON document describing which keys, types and bounds an object may have, that any language can check against. `schema_contract.py` prints a few parts of `Snapshot.model_json_schema()`:

Every rule written as a type is in it: `extra="forbid"` became `additionalProperties: False`, `NonNegativeInt` became `minimum: 0`, the id pattern is there, and the nested models sit under `$defs`. The rules written as Python code, the two model validators, are not: JSON Schema cannot say "every parent is a project", so the published document describes the structure and the service still runs the validators. FastAPI publishes the JSON Schema of every request model in its API description automatically, which is how lesson 12.4.1's service will hand this contract to the export team.

A contract changes. When the model gains a parameter, or a field is renamed, old exports must not be read as if they were new ones. That is what `schema_version: Literal[1]` is for: the field must be present and must be 1, so a document from before versions, or from a newer exporter, is refused:

no schema_version  refused: schema_version: Field required
schema_version 2   refused: schema_version: Input should be 1
An old document is not ignored or guessed at. It is brought up to date by an explicit step, one per version, before validation. Before versions existed, the export called the lag column `lag`:
version-0 export after upgrade(): accepted, P023 parent_lag = 1

Compare this with the `extra="ignore"` run above. The same renamed column, handled by a rule that knows what `lag` meant, keeps P023's lag of 1. The upgrade is code with a test, written once, and the schema stays strict.
<!-- practice 2 -->
Summary

items: **The schema is the model's sets and parameters, written as types.** Read it off the formulation: each parameter a field, each assumption a type, bound or rule.

**One schema validates the whole snapshot and reports every problem in one pass.** Field problems come first; references across records (unique ids, known parents, a budget and crews for every year) come from a model validator once the fields are clean. A snapshot that passes can be built into a model.

**At a machine boundary, forbid unknown keys and turn off guessing.** `extra="forbid"` stops a renamed key from becoming a default; `strict=True` refuses a value in the wrong JSON type. Validate the JSON text, not a dict built from it.

**The schema is a versioned contract, published as JSON Schema.** `model_json_schema()` gives the sender the structural rules; `schema_version` refuses documents of another version, and an explicit upgrade step brings old ones forward.

blocks.text: Reference

rows: a field typed as another `BaseModel`, or `tuple[Model, ...]`
`@model_validator(mode="after")`, which runs only when every field passed
one complete set of model inputs, frozen at one moment
the written rule for what a valid snapshot is: keys, types, bounds, references
convert values that can be read without loss / accept only the right JSON type
a standard, language-neutral description of a JSON document's structure

blocks.text: **Further reading:** [Pydantic: models](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/models/) (nested models, `model_validate_json`, and the `extra` setting with its `ignore` default and its per-call override); [Pydantic: strict mode](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/strict_mode/) (strict on the config, on one field, or for one validation call); [Pydantic: JSON Schema](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/json_schema/) (`model_json_schema()`, Draft 2020-12 and OpenAPI, nested models under `$defs`); [Pydantic: validators](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/validators/) (after model validators run on the validated instance and return it); [FastAPI: request body](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/body/) (a pydantic model as a request body is validated, and its JSON Schema appears in the API's OpenAPI description); [MathOpt (OR-Tools)](https://developers.google.com/optimization/math_opt) (the model API the validated snapshot is built into).
Challenges

items: A new exporter sends `"must_do": 1`. Predict what strict and lax mode each do, then check one of them with `schema_boundary.py`.
Version 2 of the contract adds a required field `crew_program` to each project. Write the upgrade step from version 1, and say what default it may safely use, if any.
The schema checks that every year in `years` has one budget row. Should it also refuse a budget row for a year outside `years`? What would the model do with one?

blocks.text: Design Note: The Schema Lives With the Model, Not With the Export

It is tempting to let the export team own the schema, since they produce the document. But every rule in it comes from the model: which parameters exist, which may be zero, which ids must resolve. When the model changes, the schema must change in the same commit, and the version with it. So the schema sits beside `plan_model.py`, and the export team receives it as JSON Schema, generated from that code, never retyped.
The Full Programs

Each snippet above is part of a complete program, and each program printed the output the lesson shows. Open one to read it whole, change it, and run it again: Run starts the program on your copy of the code, so the course's own files never change.

**schema_whole.py.** Validates GridCap small's export, then plants five field errors and four reference errors (*The Schema Is the Model's Sets and Parameters* and *One Schema Validates the Whole Snapshot*). *Try:* Remove the cost and region plants. Predict whether P016's unknown parent is reported then.

**schema_boundary.py.** The same documents under `extra="ignore"` and `"forbid"`, and under lax and strict mode (*At a Machine Boundary*). *Try:* Send the 2027 budget as `-8890`. Predict whether lax mode accepts it.

**schema_contract.py.** Prints parts of the published JSON Schema, refuses documents of other versions, and upgrades a version-0 export (*The Schema Is a Versioned Contract*). *Try:* Make `parent_lag` a required field (remove its default). Predict how `required` changes in the `ProjectIn` part of the schema.
The schema itself and the export are in `snapshot.py`, and the model in `plan_model.py`.
